ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The diagram shows a 1 MHz, 1 V modulating signal entering a balanced modulator. A 100 MHz, 1 V carrier is applied to the balanced modulator from below. The modulator output goes through an ideal high-pass filter labeled HPF, 100 MHz. The filter output is then added in a summing block to another 100 MHz, 1 V signal with 90° phase shift, producing y(t). Reasoning: Let the modulating signal be cos(ωm t), where ωm = 2π × 10^6, and let the carrier be cos(ωc t), where ωc = 2π × 10^8. The balanced modulator output is cos(ωm t) cos(ωc t). Using product-to-sum, this contains sidebands at ωc − ωm and ωc + ωm. Since the ideal HPF has cutoff 100 MHz, it removes the 99 MHz lower sideband and passes the 101 MHz upper sideband, giving (1/2) cos((ωc + ωm)t). The added 90° shifted 100 MHz signal is taken, with the phase convention matching the figure/answer, as sin(ωc t). Thus y(t) = (1/2) cos((ωc + ωm)t) + sin(ωc t). Expanding the upper sideband: (1/2) cos((ωc + ωm)t) = (1/2) cos(ωm t) cos(ωc t) − (1/2) sin(ωm t) sin(ωc t). Therefore y(t) = [(1/2) cos(ωm t)] cos(ωc t) + [1 − (1/2) sin(ωm t)] sin(ωc t). The envelope is the magnitude of the quadrature coefficient vector: sqrt{[(1/2) cos(ωm t)]^2 + [1 − (1/2) sin(ωm t)]^2} = sqrt{1/4 cos^2(ωm t) + 1 − sin(ωm t) + 1/4 sin^2(ωm t)} = sqrt{5/4 − sin(ωm t)}. Substituting ωm = 2π × 10^6 gives sqrt(5/4 − sin(2π × 10^6 t)).
